items.stem: An AI suggestion fixes a type error by changing a prop type to 'any'. Why is accepting this risky?

options.text: 'any' disables type checking for that value, hiding real errors
options.rationale: Correct: using 'any' removes the safety the type system provides.
'any' is valid; the problem is that it removes checking.

options.text: Changing a prop type is impossible
options.rationale: It is possible; the concern is losing type safety.

options.text: Type errors never matter in React
options.rationale: Type errors can cause real runtime defects.

items.stem: Which TWO practices keep AI-assisted frontend work trustworthy? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run the tests before accepting a multi-file AI edit
options.rationale: Correct: tests guard against regressions the edit introduces.

options.text: Give the model the relevant files and project patterns as context
options.rationale: Correct: good context yields output that fits the codebase.

options.text: Merge generated code without any human reading it
options.rationale: A human must remain accountable for merged code.

options.text: Silence type errors to move faster

items.explanation: Correct: tests guard against regressions the edit introduces.

items.stem: Who is accountable for a defect in AI-generated code that was merged?

options.text: The human who reviewed and merged it
options.rationale: Correct: accountability stays with the person who approves and merges the code.
The tool assists; it does not take responsibility for merged code.

options.text: No one, because AI wrote it
options.rationale: Human accountability does not disappear when AI assists.

options.text: The end user who hit the bug
options.rationale: Users are not accountable for the code that ships.

items.explanation: Correct: accountability stays with the person who approves and merges the code.
